questions.q: What are the materials that are attracted towards a magnet called?
questions.a: Magnetic materials
o: Magnetic materials
Non-magnetic materials
Lodestones
Poles

questions.q: Before testing with a magnet, Manu predicted that a nickel washer, a wooden spoon, a rubber band and a cobalt strip would ALL stick to it, because all four feel hard. After he tests them, how many of his four predictions turn out to be correct?
questions.a: 2, as only the nickel washer and the cobalt strip stick
o: 2, as only the nickel washer and the cobalt strip stick
4, as hard objects are always attracted towards a magnet
1, as only an object made of iron sticks to a magnet
3, as every object except the rubber band sticks

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Magnetic material  2. Non-magnetic material  3. Lodestone  4. Artificial magnet
Column II: A. A naturally occurring magnet, used by sailors in olden days  B. A magnet made by people, like the one in a pencil box  C. A material not attracted towards a magnet, such as rubber  D. A material attracted towards a magnet, such as cobalt

Assertion (A): A wooden pencil does not move towards a magnet brought near it.
Reason (R): The magnets used in pencil boxes, stickers and toys are artificial magnets.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What are non-magnetic materials? (b) Name one magnetic metal other than iron.
questions.a: (a) Materials that are not attracted towards a magnet are called non-magnetic materials. (b) Nickel (cobalt is also correct).
s: (a) States that non-magnetic materials are not attracted towards a magnet
(b) Names nickel or cobalt

questions.q: True or False? 'Iron is the only metal that is attracted towards a magnet.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Nickel and cobalt are also magnetic metals, and some of their combinations with other metals are attracted towards a magnet too.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: nickel and cobalt (and some of their combinations with other metals) are also attracted

questions.q: Ayaan brings a magnet near four objects, one by one: an iron bolt, a nickel washer, a rubber slipper and a wooden comb. (a) Which objects will stick to the magnet? (b) What name is given to the materials that the other objects are made of? (c) Name one more metal, not in his list, that would also stick to the magnet.
questions.a: (a) The iron bolt and the nickel washer. (b) Non-magnetic materials. (c) Cobalt.
s: (a) Names the iron bolt and the nickel washer
(b) Calls rubber and wood non-magnetic materials
(c) Names cobalt

questions.q: In Reshma's classroom, a duster with a magnet fixed on its back stays stuck on the writing board, but slides off and falls when it is placed on the wooden door. (a) What can you conclude about the material inside the writing board? (b) Why does the duster not stay on the door? (c) The teacher covers the writing board with a thin plastic sheet. Will the duster still stay on the board? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The board must contain a magnetic material (such as iron) that the magnet is attracted towards. (b) Wood is a non-magnetic material, so the magnet is not attracted towards the door. (c) Yes. The magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as thin plastic, so the magnet is still attracted towards the magnetic material inside the board.
s: (a) Concludes that the board contains a magnetic material such as iron
(b) Explains that wood is non-magnetic, so there is no attraction
(c) Says yes, because the magnetic effect acts through thin plastic, a non-magnetic material

questions.q:
Mrs Thomas gives her class a tray holding a rubber ball, an iron hair clip, a cobalt strip and a wooden ruler, along with a bar magnet. Answer each part.
(a) Which two objects in the tray will stick to the magnet?
(b) What are the materials of these two objects called?
(c) Write what is meant by non-magnetic materials.
(d) Name one magnetic metal that is not in the tray.
(e) She now adds a key made by mixing nickel with another metal. Can the class be sure, without testing, that it will stick to the magnet? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The iron hair clip and the cobalt strip. (b) Magnetic materials. (c) Materials that are not attracted towards a magnet. (d) Nickel. (e) No. The chapter says only SOME combinations of nickel or cobalt with other metals are attracted towards magnets, so the key must be tested.
s: (a) Names the iron hair clip and the cobalt strip
(b) Calls them magnetic materials
(c) States that non-magnetic materials are not attracted towards a magnet
(d) Names nickel
(e) Says no, because only some combinations of nickel with other metals are attracted, so it must be tested

questions.q:
At her school fair, Reshma runs a 'Will it stick?' stall. Each of 40 visitors first predicts Yes or No for five objects and then tests them with a magnet. The number of visitors who predicted 'Yes, it will stick' was: iron key 37, nickel washer 12, cobalt strip 15, wooden ruler 3, rubber ball 2.
(a) Which of the five objects actually stick to the magnet?
(b) How many visitors predicted correctly for the cobalt strip?
(c) For which object did the largest number of visitors predict wrongly, and how many were wrong?
(d) Next year Reshma has space for only one metal object. She wants it to surprise the most visitors and to teach that iron is not the only magnetic metal. Which object should she keep? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) The iron key, the nickel washer and the cobalt strip. (b) 15 visitors (those who said Yes). (c) The nickel washer: 40 - 12 = 28 visitors wrongly said No (cobalt strip 25, iron key 3, wooden ruler 3, rubber ball 2). (d) The nickel washer. It is a magnetic metal other than iron, and it surprised the most visitors (28 wrong, more than the 25 for the cobalt strip and far more than the 3 for the iron key).
s: (a) Names the iron key, nickel washer and cobalt strip
(b) Gives 15
(c) Names the nickel washer with 28 wrong predictions
(d) Chooses the nickel washer, using 28 > 25 > 3 and that it is not iron

questions.q: A bar magnet is placed over iron filings spread on a sheet of paper, and the paper is tapped. Where do most of the iron filings stick?
questions.a: Near the two ends of the magnet
o: Near the two ends of the magnet
At the middle of the magnet
Evenly all along the length of the magnet
Only at the North pole end

questions.q: A ring magnet falls off a toy and breaks into two halves. Which statement about the two halves is correct?
questions.a: Each half has a North pole and a South pole
o: Each half has a North pole and a South pole
One half has only a North pole, the other only a South pole
Neither half has any pole left after breaking
Only the bigger half still has two poles

questions.q: A long bar magnet snaps into three pieces. Later, one of those pieces snaps again into two. How many North poles are there in all the pieces taken together?

Consider the following statements.
I. Most iron filings stick to the poles of a magnet, whatever the shape of the magnet.
II. Lodestones were made by people from pieces of iron.
III. A cylindrical magnet has both a North pole and a South pole.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Each piece of a broken bar magnet attracts iron filings mostly near its two ends.
Reason (R): North and South poles always exist in pairs, even in the smallest piece of a magnet.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What are the poles of a magnet? (b) Name the two poles of a magnet.
questions.a: (a) The poles are the parts of a magnet where most iron filings stick; for a bar magnet they are its two ends. (b) The North pole and the South pole.
s: (a) Says the poles are where most iron filings stick (the ends of a bar magnet)
(b) Names the North pole and the South pole

questions.q: Tejas places an irregular lump of lodestone on iron filings and taps the paper. The filings collect thickly at two places on the lump. (a) What are these two places? (b) Can Tejas tell from the filings alone which of the two places is the North pole? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) They are the two poles of the lodestone, its North pole and its South pole. (b) No. Most iron filings stick at both poles, so the filings show where the poles are but not which one is North. He needs another test, such as hanging the lodestone freely.
s: (a) Identifies the two places as the two poles (North and South)
(b) Says no, because filings cluster at both poles alike, so another test is needed

questions.q: Zoya's teacher spreads iron filings on a sheet of paper and places a bar magnet over them. (a) What are iron filings? (b) On which part of the bar magnet do very few filings stick? (c) Zoya asks whether a magnet can ever have only a North pole. What should the teacher answer?
questions.a: (a) Very small pieces of iron. (b) The remaining part of the magnet away from its ends, that is, its middle part. (c) No. A magnet with a single pole cannot be obtained; North and South poles always exist in pairs.
s: (a) Says iron filings are very small pieces of iron
(b) Names the middle part, away from the ends
(c) Says no, because poles always exist in pairs

questions.q: Kiran breaks an old bar magnet into two pieces and dips each piece into iron filings. In his notebook he writes: 'Piece 1 collected filings thickly at only ONE of its ends; its other end and its middle collected almost none.' Show that this record cannot be right for a piece of a magnet.
questions.a: Each piece of a broken magnet is itself a magnet with both a North pole and a South pole, because poles always exist in pairs. Most iron filings stick at the poles, so a bar-shaped piece should collect filings thickly near BOTH its ends. Filings thick at only one end would mean a magnet with a single pole, which cannot exist, so the record must be wrong.
s: States that each broken piece has both a North and a South pole
Uses the fact that most filings stick at both poles, so both ends should collect filings
Concludes that one-end-only would mean a single pole, which is impossible

questions.q:
Pooja's school science kit has a bar magnet, a U-shaped magnet and a ring magnet. Answer step by step.
(a) How many poles does each magnet have, and what are they called?
(b) Where will most iron filings stick on the bar magnet?
(c) The bar magnet breaks into two pieces. How many poles are there now in the two pieces together?
(d) Are the kit magnets natural or artificial? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Each magnet has two poles, a North pole and a South pole. (b) Near its two ends. (c) 4 poles, because each piece has its own North and South pole. (d) Artificial: magnets found in a school laboratory are artificial magnets; natural magnets are lodestones.
s: (a) Says each has two poles, North and South
(b) Says near the two ends
(c) Gives 4 poles, two in each piece
(d) Says artificial, as school laboratory magnets are made by people while lodestones are natural

questions.q: Along which direction does a freely suspended bar magnet come to rest?
questions.a: North-south
o: North-south
East-west
Any direction, changing each time
North-east to south-west

questions.q: Hari hangs a bar magnet by a thread tied at its middle. When it comes to rest, end X points towards the south. What is end X called?
questions.a: The South-seeking pole
o: The South-seeking pole
The North-seeking pole
The middle of the magnet
A neutral end with no pole

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about hanging bars freely by a thread.
I. A small plain iron bar hung freely by its middle can come to rest along any direction.
II. The end of a hung magnet that points towards the south is called its North-seeking pole.
III. A hung magnet given a fresh gentle push comes to rest along a different line each time.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I only
o: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A small plain iron bar, hung freely by a thread tied at its middle, always comes to rest along the north-south direction.
Reason (R): Iron is a magnetic material.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: True or False? 'Hanging a piece of metal freely and watching the direction in which it comes to rest can tell us whether it is a magnet.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Only a magnet always comes to rest along the north-south direction; a plain iron bar can rest along any direction. So repeating the test shows whether the metal is a magnet.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: only a magnet always rests north-south, while a plain iron bar can rest along any direction

questions.q: In the activity of hanging a bar magnet from a thread: (a) Why is the thread tied at the middle of the magnet and adjusted until the magnet hangs level? (b) What does the line joining the two marked ends of the resting magnet on the ground show?
questions.a: (a) So that the magnet is balanced horizontally and can rotate freely in the horizontal direction. (b) The direction along which the magnet comes to rest, which is the north-south direction.
s: (a) States that the magnet is balanced horizontally so that it can rotate freely
(b) States that the line shows the north-south direction

questions.q: As a prank, Ajay's little sister paints the SOUTH pole of his bar magnet red, but Ajay believes that red always marks the North pole. He hangs the magnet freely from a thread in the school ground. (a) In which direction will the red end point when the magnet comes to rest? (b) Ajay walks the way the red end points, thinking he is going north. In which direction is he really walking? (c) Ajay noticed where the Sun rose that morning. Without another magnet or a compass, how can he find which end of the magnet is really the North-seeking pole?
questions.a: (a) South, because the red end is the South pole, and the South-seeking pole of a freely suspended magnet points south. (b) South, the opposite of what he thinks. (c) The direction of sunrise gives him an approximate idea of east, and so of where north and south lie; the end of the resting magnet that points towards north is the North-seeking pole, whatever its paint.
s: (a) Says the red end points south, because it is the South pole
(b) Says he is really walking south
(c) Uses sunrise to get an approximate idea of east and so of north, then names the end pointing north as the North-seeking pole

questions.q:
A Class 6 group camps for five days in Munnar. Their notes say the sky was clear at sunrise on only 2 of the 5 mornings, and the nights were overcast on 4 of the 5 nights. They have a bar magnet with its North pole painted red, some thread, and know that the place where the Sun rises gives an approximate idea of east.
(a) On how many of the five mornings could they use the Sun to get an idea of direction?
(b) How should they hang the magnet so that it can turn freely?
(c) In which direction will the red end point once the magnet comes to rest?
(d) Why does the hung magnet work even on an overcast night?
(e) For a night walk on the sixth day, which method should the group rely on? Justify using the data.
questions.a: (a) On 2 mornings. (b) Tie the thread at the middle of the magnet and adjust it till the magnet is balanced horizontally. (c) North. (d) A freely suspended magnet rests along north-south because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet; it does not need the Sun or the stars to be seen. (e) The hung magnet: the Sun method worked on only 2 of 5 mornings and cannot be used at night at all, while the magnet works in clear or cloudy weather, by day or night.
s: (a) Gives 2 mornings
(b) Thread tied at the middle, magnet balanced horizontally
(c) Says the red (North) end points north
(d) Explains that the Earth behaves like a giant magnet, so no Sun or stars are needed
(e) Chooses the hung magnet, using 2 of 5 mornings and no use at night for the Sun method

questions.q:
On a school trip to Wayanad, Class 6 students tie a thread to the middle of an unmarked metal bar and hang it from a branch so that it hangs level. They give it a gentle push four times. Every time it comes to rest, end P points towards the hilltop and end Q points towards the river. Their teacher's map shows that the hilltop lies to the north of the camp. Next they hang a plain iron bar from the tent kit in the same way: it stops facing the river once, the tent twice and the road once.
(a) Is the first bar a magnet? Give the evidence from the passage.
(b) What is end P called?
(c) In which direction from the camp does the river lie?
(d) Why did the plain iron bar not point the same way every time?
questions.a: (a) Yes. It came to rest along the same line every time, as a freely suspended magnet does. (b) The North-seeking pole (North pole), because it points north. (c) South, because end Q, the South-seeking pole, points towards the river. (d) A plain iron bar is not a magnet, so it does not rest along north-south; it can come to rest along any direction.
s: (a) Says yes, because it rested along the same line every time
(b) Names end P the North-seeking (North) pole
(c) Says the river lies to the south
(d) Explains that a plain iron bar is not a magnet and can rest along any direction

questions.q:
In Reshma's story, sailors caught in a storm, with no stars visible, find their way using a lodestone hung by a thread. Explain in four steps why this idea works.
(a) What is a lodestone?
(b) How must the lodestone be hung so that it can turn freely?
(c) Along which direction will it come to rest, and why?
(d) On a clear night before the storm, one sailor used the stars to mark the end of the lodestone that settles pointing north. Why is this mark useful during the storm?
questions.a: (a) A naturally occurring magnet; the magnets of sailors in olden days were based on lodestones. (b) Hung by a thread and balanced so that it can rotate freely in the horizontal direction. (c) Along the north-south direction, because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet. (d) The resting lodestone only gives the north-south line; the mark tells the sailors which end is the North-seeking pole, so they know which way along that line is north even when no stars can be seen.
s: (a) Defines a lodestone as a naturally occurring magnet
(b) Hung by a thread and balanced so it rotates freely
(c) Rests north-south because the Earth behaves like a giant magnet
(d) Explains that the mark shows which end is the North-seeking pole, so north can be told apart from south

questions.q: In a magnetic compass, the end of the needle that rests in the north direction is usually painted:
questions.a: red
o: red
blue
white
green

questions.q: What was the matsya-yantra, used by Indians for navigation at sea?
questions.a: A magnetised fish-shaped iron piece kept in a vessel of oil
o: A magnetised fish-shaped iron piece kept in a vessel of oil
A fish-shaped lodestone hung by a thread from the mast
A fish-shaped needle mounted on a pin inside a box with a dial
A wooden fish that floats and drifts towards the north

questions.q: The matsya-yantra and the needle compass that a student makes with a cork in a bowl of water look very different. What is the main thing they share that lets both of them show directions?
questions.a: Each has a magnetised iron piece that floats on a liquid and can turn freely
o: Each has a magnetised iron piece that floats on a liquid and can turn freely
Each needs a fish shape so that it can point along the flow of the water around it
Each uses a liquid that is itself magnetic and pulls the iron to the north
Each uses a lodestone, because iron can never be made into a magnet

questions.q:
Match each part of a magnetic compass in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Needle  2. Pin  3. Dial  4. Red-painted end
Column II: A. Rests pointing towards the north  B. A magnet that indicates the north-south direction  C. Lies below the needle and has directions marked on it  D. Stands on the bottom of the box; the needle is balanced on it so that it can rotate freely
True or False? 'Long before the modern magnetic compass came into wide use, Indians used a device similar to a needle-and-cork compass for navigation at sea.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The matsya-yantra, a magnetised fish-shaped iron piece kept in a vessel of oil, was used by Indians for navigation at sea much before the widespread use of the modern magnetic compass.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: names the matsya-yantra, a magnetised fish-shaped iron piece in a vessel of oil, used at sea

questions.q: In the activity of making your own compass with a sewing needle: (a) At least how many times is the needle stroked with the magnet? (b) How do you check that the needle has become a magnet?
questions.a: (a) At least 30 to 40 times. (b) Bring iron filings or steel pins near the needle; if they are attracted to it, the needle has become a magnet.
s: (a) States at least 30 to 40 times
(b) Says that iron filings or steel pins brought near get attracted to it

questions.q: In Reshma's story, a ship carrying spices from Kerala is caught in a storm at night. (a) How did sailors in those days usually find directions at night? (b) Why could they not do so during this storm? (c) Name the magnet-based device that travellers used for finding directions, and the property of a magnet on which it is based.
questions.a: (a) By looking at the stars. (b) The sky was overcast, so the stars were not visible. (c) The magnetic compass; it is based on the property that a freely suspended magnet always rests along the north-south direction.
s: (a) Says they used the stars
(b) Says the overcast sky hid the stars
(c) Names the magnetic compass and the property that a freely suspended magnet rests north-south

questions.q: Tanu says, 'The matsya-yantra worked only because its iron fish was kept in oil. The oil must be the magnetic part that turned the fish towards the north.' Check her claim, using what you know about the needle compass you can make in class.
questions.a: Her claim is not correct. In the needle compass made in class, the magnetised needle floats on a cork in water, not oil, and it still settles in the same direction every time. So the liquid is not what makes it point; it only supports the iron piece so that it can turn freely. The pointing comes from the magnetised iron (the fish or the needle), which, like any freely suspended magnet, rests along north-south.
s: Notes that the class needle compass uses water, not oil, and still points the same way
Explains that the liquid only lets the iron piece float and turn freely
Concludes that the magnetised iron is what points north-south, so the claim is wrong

questions.q:
A museum in Kochi will place three direction-finders side by side: a matsya-yantra, a needle compass floating on a cork in water, and a modern magnetic compass. Write a four-point note for the display.
(a) State the one idea that makes all three work.
(b) State how the magnet is supported so that it can turn freely in each device.
(c) Which device is closest in design to the matsya-yantra? Justify.
(d) Name one part of the modern compass, described in the chapter, that lets a user read all the directions, and say how it is used.
questions.a: (a) Each has a magnet (magnetised iron) that can turn freely, and a freely turning magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction. (b) Matsya-yantra: the fish-shaped iron piece is kept in a vessel of oil. Needle compass: the needle is passed through a cork floating on water. Modern compass: the needle is balanced on a pin standing on the bottom of the box. (c) The needle compass on a cork, because in both the magnetised iron is supported on a liquid; the chapter itself calls the matsya-yantra a device similar to it. (d) The dial below the needle: after the needle comes to rest, the box is turned until N and S on the dial line up with the needle, and then all the directions can be read off the dial.
s: (a) States that a freely turning magnet rests north-south
(b) Gives the support in all three: oil, cork on water, pin
(c) Chooses the cork-and-needle compass, as both float on a liquid
(d) Names the dial and describes turning the box to line up N and S with the needle

questions.q:
At a scout camp in Bhopal, Imran sets his compass on top of his school bag. His bag holds a pencil box that is kept shut by a magnet. Three readings are taken, each after the needle has come to rest:
Reading 1: compass on Imran's bag; the red end points towards the water tank.
Reading 2: Imran's compass on bare ground, 3 m away from the bag; the red end points towards the flagpole.
Reading 3: another scout's compass on bare ground; the red end points towards the flagpole.
(a) Which object, the water tank or the flagpole, lies to the north of the compasses? Justify using the readings.
(b) What in Imran's bag most likely disturbed Reading 1, and how could it do so?
(c) Why must the compass be left until the needle comes to rest before any reading is taken?
(d) Once the needle rests pointing at the flagpole, what must Imran do with the compass box before he reads other directions?
(e) Suggest one rule the troop should follow when using compasses, and give a reason from this camp.
questions.a: (a) The flagpole. Readings 2 and 3, taken away from the bag by two different compasses, agree; only Reading 1, taken on the bag, differs. (b) The magnet in the pencil box. The compass needle is itself a magnet, so the pencil-box magnet attracts or repels its poles (unlike poles attract, like poles repel) and turns it away from north-south. (c) Only a needle at rest has settled along north-south; a swinging needle does not show the direction. (d) Gently rotate the box until the N and S marks on the dial line up with the needle; then read the other directions off the dial. (e) Keep the compass away from magnets, such as pencil boxes or bags with magnets, because a nearby magnet deflects the needle, as it did in Reading 1.
s: (a) Chooses the flagpole because Readings 2 and 3 agree away from the bag
(b) Names the pencil-box magnet and explains attraction or repulsion of the needle's poles
(c) Explains that only a resting needle shows north-south
(d) Turns the box till N and S on the dial line up with the needle
(e) Gives the rule to keep compasses away from magnets, with Reading 1 as the reason

questions.q: Which pair of magnet poles attract each other?
questions.a: A North pole and a South pole
o: A North pole and a South pole
A North pole and a North pole
A South pole and a South pole
No pair; magnet poles only repel

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a safe way to treat magnets?
questions.a: Keeping a magnet next to a mobile phone
o: Keeping a magnet next to a mobile phone
Storing two magnets with unlike poles on the same side
Placing soft iron pieces across the ends of a stored pair
Keeping a piece of wood between two stored magnets

questions.q: Two bar magnets lie in a line on a table and pull together, with the North pole of magnet 1 facing end X of magnet 2. Gopi turns magnet 1 round so that its other end now faces end X. What happens now?
questions.a: They push apart, as end X is a South pole and faces a South pole
o: They push apart, as end X is a South pole and faces a South pole
They still pull together, as two magnets always attract each other
They pull together harder, as both poles of magnet 1 attract X
Nothing happens, as turning a magnet round removes its poles

questions.q:
Read these statements about keeping magnets safe.
I. Two bar magnets should be stored in a pair with their like poles on the same side.
II. A piece of wood is kept between the two magnets of a stored pair.
III. A magnet can be hammered into a new shape without any harm to it.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: II only
o: II only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When the North pole of a bar magnet is brought slowly near the North end of a compass needle, the needle's North end moves away.
Reason (R): Like poles of magnets repel each other, and the compass needle is itself a magnet.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'A plain iron bar is repelled by one of the poles of a bar magnet.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Both ends of a plain iron bar are attracted by both the North and the South pole of a magnet; an iron bar is never repelled. Only another magnet can be repelled.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: both ends of an iron bar are attracted by both poles; only a magnet can be repelled

questions.q: Sneha brings end E1 of an unmarked bar magnet slowly near the North end of a resting compass needle, and the North end moves away. Then she brings the other end, E2, near the same North end, and it moves closer. (a) Name the poles at E1 and E2. (b) Predict what the South end of the needle will do when E1 is brought near it, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) E1 is a North pole (like poles repel) and E2 is a South pole (unlike poles attract). (b) The South end of the needle will move closer to E1, because a North pole and a South pole are unlike poles, which attract.
s: (a) Names E1 North and E2 South, using like repel and unlike attract
(b) Predicts the South end moves closer, as unlike poles attract

questions.q: A bar magnet hangs freely from a thread and has come to rest along north-south. Pinky slowly brings the North pole of a second bar magnet near the hung magnet's North-seeking end, and later near its South-seeking end. (a) What happens the first time? (b) What happens the second time? (c) Pinky then takes the second magnet far away. How will the hung magnet finally come to rest?
questions.a: (a) The North-seeking end turns away from the second magnet, because like poles repel. (b) The South-seeking end turns towards the second magnet, because unlike poles attract. (c) It comes to rest along the north-south direction again, with its North-seeking end pointing north.
s: (a) North-seeking end turns away, as like poles repel
(b) South-seeking end turns towards it, as unlike poles attract
(c) It again rests north-south with the North-seeking end pointing north

questions.q:
Four bars K, L, M and N look exactly alike. Three are magnets and one is a plain iron bar. Ravi tests them in pairs; in each test he tries BOTH ends of one bar against one end of the other and notes whether the two bars ever push apart.
K and L: pushed apart once.
K and M: only pulled together.
L and M: only pulled together.
L and N: pushed apart once.
(a) Which tests prove that both bars in the pair are magnets?
(b) Which bar is the plain iron bar?
(c) In the K and M test, explain why 'only pulled together' shows that M is not a magnet.
(d) Does Ravi still need to test K with N to find out whether N is a magnet? Explain.
(e) Ravi brings M near the North end of a resting compass needle. Predict what the needle's North end does, and why.
questions.a: (a) K with L and L with N, because repulsion happens only between two magnets. So K, L and N are magnets. (b) M. (c) K is a magnet. If M were also a magnet, one of M's two ends would have faced K with a like pole and the bars would have pushed apart; a plain iron bar is attracted by both poles of a magnet and is never repelled. (d) No. The L and N test already showed repulsion, which proves that N is a magnet. (e) It moves closer to M, because the needle is a magnet and a magnet attracts a plain iron bar with both its poles.
s: (a) Names the K-L and L-N tests, as repulsion happens only between magnets
(b) Names M as the plain iron bar
(c) Explains that a magnet M would have repelled K with one end, but plain iron is never repelled
(d) Says no, because the L-N repulsion already proves N is a magnet
(e) Predicts the North end moves closer, as a magnet attracts iron

questions.q:
A toy factory in Channapatna receives a box of 200 unmarked bars and must paint the North pole of each magnet red. By mistake, 8 of the 200 bars are plain iron bars; the other 192 are magnets. Each worker has one reference magnet with its North and South poles marked. Worker A paints red only the end that pushes away the reference magnet's North pole. Worker B paints red the end that is pulled towards the reference magnet's South pole.
(a) Explain why the end that Worker A paints red is really a North pole.
(b) What will Worker B do with each plain iron bar, and why?
(c) What percentage of the bars in the box were not magnets?
(d) Which worker's method should the factory use for all its boxes? Justify using (a)-(c).
questions.a: (a) It pushes away the reference North pole, and like poles repel, so it is a North pole. (b) He will paint one end of it red, because both ends of a plain iron bar are pulled towards the South pole (and the North pole) of a magnet; he cannot tell that it is not a magnet. (c) 8/200 x 100 = 4%. (d) Worker A's method: repulsion happens only with a magnet, so the 8 iron bars (4% of the box) never push away and are left unpainted, while Worker B's attraction test wrongly paints all of them.
s: (a) Explains that like poles repel, so the end is North
(b) Says B paints an end red on each iron bar, since iron is attracted by both poles
(c) Calculates 4%
(d) Chooses Worker A, as only repulsion identifies a magnet and catches the 4% iron bars

questions.q: Sheets of wood, cardboard, thin plastic and thin glass were placed, one at a time, between a magnet and a compass needle. What did this activity show?
questions.a: The magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials
o: The magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials
The sheets became magnets and pushed the needle away
Every non-magnetic sheet blocks the magnetic effect completely
Only the glass sheet let the magnetic effect pass

questions.q: The North pole of a bar magnet has made the North end of a compass needle move away. Without moving the compass, which ONE of these changes will noticeably change the position of the needle?
questions.a: Turning the magnet round so that its South pole faces the needle
o: Turning the magnet round so that its South pole faces the needle
Standing a thin cardboard sheet upright between the magnet and the compass
Standing a thin plastic sheet upright between the two
Standing a piece of wood upright between the two

questions.q:
Match each set-up in Column I with what is observed in Column II.
Column I: 1. A thin plastic sheet is placed between a magnet and a compass needle  2. The North pole of a magnet is brought near the North end of a compass needle  3. The South pole of a magnet is brought near the North end of a compass needle  4. Either pole of a magnet is brought near a plain iron bar
Column II: A. The needle's North end moves closer  B. No appreciable change in the needle's deflection  C. The needle's North end moves away  D. The iron bar is attracted

Assertion (A): A compass needle is still deflected by a magnet when a cardboard sheet stands between them.
Reason (R): Cardboard is a magnetic material.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name any two materials that were placed between a magnet and a compass needle to test whether the magnetic effect passes through them. (b) What change did these materials make to the deflection of the needle?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: wood, cardboard, thin plastic sheet, thin glass sheet. (b) No appreciable change in the deflection.
s: (a) Names any two of wood, cardboard, thin plastic, thin glass
(b) States there was no appreciable change in the deflection

questions.q: Rahul says, 'Wood is non-magnetic, so a piece of wood standing between a magnet and a compass needle must weaken the magnet's effect on the needle a lot.' (a) What does the needle actually do when the wood is placed? (b) Correct Rahul's reasoning.
questions.a: (a) There is no appreciable change in its deflection. (b) 'Non-magnetic' only means that wood is not attracted towards a magnet. It does not mean wood stops the magnetic effect; the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as wood.
s: (a) States no appreciable change in the deflection
(b) Explains that non-magnetic means not attracted, not that it blocks the effect, which passes through wood

questions.q: A toy boat with a steel pin fixed under it floats in a plastic tub of water. Arya slowly moves a magnet along below the tub, outside it. (a) What happens to the boat? (b) Which idea from the chapter explains this?
questions.a: (a) The boat moves along with the magnet. (b) The magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as plastic, so the magnet still attracts the steel pin.
s: (a) Says the boat follows the magnet
(b) States that the magnetic effect acts through the non-magnetic plastic and attracts the steel pin

questions.q: Aman says, 'The magnetic effect passes through wood, so a magnet moved under a wooden table will drag along both the steel pin and the wooden bead lying on top of the table.' Check his claim.
questions.a: He is partly right. The steel pin will move: steel is attracted by a magnet, and the magnetic effect acts through the non-magnetic wood of the table. The wooden bead will not move: wood is a non-magnetic material, so the magnet does not attract it at all. The effect passing through a material does not make non-magnetic objects get pulled; only magnetic materials are pulled.
s: Says the steel pin moves, as the effect acts through the wooden table
Says the wooden bead does not move, as wood is non-magnetic and is not attracted
Gives the verdict partly right: acting through a material does not make non-magnetic things get pulled

questions.q:
Reshma's class has Rs 250 to set up stalls at the school fair. Each stall needs its own materials.
Stall A, 'Magic maze': a cardboard tray Rs 30, six steel balls at Rs 10 each, one bar magnet Rs 50.
Stall B, 'Rescue the clip': a glass bowl Rs 70, steel paper clips Rs 20, one bar magnet Rs 50.
Stall C, 'Racing cars': two matchboxes Rs 10 in all, two bar magnets at Rs 50 each.
(a) Why do the steel balls in stall A move when the magnet is moved below the tray?
(b) How can a clip lying in the water of stall B be brought out without wetting the magnet or one's fingers?
(c) In stall C, the two cars carry magnets with like poles facing each other. What do the cars do when brought close?
(d) Find the cost of each stall.
(e) Water is not allowed in the hall, and the class wants two stalls that show two different ideas about magnets. Which two stalls should they set up within Rs 250? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The magnetic effect acts through the non-magnetic cardboard, so the magnet attracts the steel balls through the tray. (b) Hold the magnet against the outside of the glass bowl near the clip and slide it up to the rim; the magnetic effect acts through the non-magnetic glass, so the steel clip is attracted and follows the magnet up the side. (c) They move away from each other, because like poles repel. (d) A: 30 + 6 x 10 + 50 = Rs 140. B: 70 + 20 + 50 = Rs 140. C: 10 + 2 x 50 = Rs 110. (e) Stalls A and C: together they cost 140 + 110 = Rs 250, which is within the budget, and they show two different ideas (acting through non-magnetic materials, and like poles repelling). B needs water, and A with B would cost Rs 280 and show the same idea twice.
s: (a) Explains the effect acts through the cardboard and attracts steel
(b) Slides the magnet up the outside of the bowl, as the effect acts through glass
(c) Says the cars move apart, as like poles repel
(d) Finds Rs 140, Rs 140 and Rs 110
(e) Chooses A and C for Rs 250, rejecting B for water and A with B for cost and same idea

questions.q:
An aquarium shop in Kozhikode sells two cleaners for small fish tanks with thin glass walls. In each, a scrubber pad sits inside the water against the glass, and the user slides an outer pad, which holds a magnet, along the outside of the glass. In model P the inside pad also holds a magnet; in model Q the inside pad holds a plain steel plate. Last year the shop sold 120 of each model. 18 model P cleaners and 3 model Q cleaners came back with the complaint that the inside pad 'jumps away and sinks' when it is placed.
(a) Why does the inside pad follow the outer pad, even though there is glass between them?
(b) In model P, what happens if the inside pad is placed the wrong way round, and why?
(c) What percentage of each model came back?
(d) A first-time buyer asks which model to choose. Which should the shopkeeper recommend? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as glass, so the outer magnet still attracts the inside pad. (b) If like poles of the two magnets face each other through the glass, they repel, so the inside pad is pushed away and sinks. (c) Model P: 18/120 x 100 = 15%. Model Q: 3/120 x 100 = 2.5%. (d) Model Q. A steel plate is attracted by either pole of a magnet, so it cannot be placed the wrong way round, and its return rate (2.5%) is far lower than model P's (15%).
s: (a) Explains the magnetic effect acts through the glass
(b) Says like poles facing repel and push the inside pad away
(c) Calculates 15% and 2.5%
(d) Recommends model Q, as steel is attracted either way round and 2.5% < 15%
